steps.label: Addition Rules
steps.content:
Addition Rules

  • Binary addition works column by column, right to left, just like denary addition.
  • Add the two bits in a column plus any carry that arrived from the column to the right.
  • A total of 2 means write 0 and carry 1 to the next column.
  • A total of 3 means write 1 and carry 1 to the next column.
Column totalWriteCarry
0 + 000
0 + 110
1 + 101
1 + 1 + 111

steps.label: Carry Chains
steps.content:
Carry Chains

  • A carry chain happens when a carry lands on a column that is also a 1, producing another carry.
  • The chain keeps moving left as long as it keeps landing on 1s.
  • The chain stops the first time it lands on a column where both bits are 0, that column becomes a 1 with nothing left to carry.
  • Adding 1 to a run of 1s, like 00001111, always produces a carry chain.

steps.label: Check Your Understanding
steps.content:
Check Your Understanding

Questions to ask around the room:

  • What do you write when a column total is 2? What about 3?
  • Which direction do you work when adding binary columns?
  • What is a carry chain, and what makes it stop?
  • Why can adding just 1 to 00001111 change four digits at once?
  • What happens to a carry that comes out of the leftmost column?

steps.label: Overflow
steps.content:
Overflow

An 8-bit register has eight columns and no more. Adding two large numbers can produce a carry out of the leftmost column, and that carry has nowhere to go.

  • The leftmost column in an 8-bit number is the 128s column.
  • If addition produces a carry out of the 128s column, the register cannot store it.
  • That carry is lost. This is called overflow.
  • The stored result is 256 less than the true total.

Worked example: 200 + 100

200 is 11001000. 100 is 01100100. The true total is 300, which needs 9 bits to store.

Adding the two 8-bit numbers produces a carry out of the 128s column. That carry is lost, so the register stores 00101100, which is 44.

300 minus 256 is 44, matching the stored result.
